opus-5.5.text:
I'd say they clarified it in two complementary directions. One is about breadth, the other is about depth.

With π0.5, the question we were really asking was: can a robot walk into a home it has never seen and do something useful? Not a lab, not a staged tabletop, but a real kitchen or bedroom with its own clutter and layout. The answer was a qualified yes, and what made it work wasn't one trick. It was the recipe of co-training on very heterogeneous data: data from many different robots, mobile manipulation data from lots of different homes, web data for semantic understanding, and high-level language annotations so the model could break a task like "clean the kitchen" into subtasks. The lesson was that generalization in robotics, like in language, comes from diversity of data more than from piling up more of the same demonstration. Once that diversity is there, you start to see the model handle new objects and new environments in a way that felt qualitatively different from before.

But π0.5 also made the limitation very clear. Generalizing is not the same as being good at the task. The robot could attempt things in a new home, but the success rate, speed, and robustness weren't at the level where you'd want to deploy it and leave it alone. Imitation learning basically caps you at the quality of your demonstrations, and actually below that, because small errors compound and the model has never seen how to recover from its own mistakes.

That's where π*0.6 comes in. The core idea is learning from experience. The robot is deployed, it practices, it gets feedback, sometimes from a human stepping in with corrections, sometimes from whether the episode succeeded or not, and we use that to train a value function. The policy is then conditioned on how good an action is expected to be, so it can learn from both good and bad experiences instead of only copying clean demos. On tasks like making espresso, folding a wide variety of laundry, or assembling boxes, that loop made a big difference in throughput and in how often things failed. It's the difference between a robot that can do the task in a demo and one that can do it for hours.

So if I put the two together, the frontier in 2025 became much sharper. It's not just "can a big model control a robot?" We know it can. The open questions are: how do you get broad generalization and high reliability in the same system, and how do you make the experience loop scale, so that every deployed robot is also collecting data that makes the next model better? To me that's the shape of the problem now. Foundation models give you the prior, and real-world reinforcement learning is what turns that prior into competence. A lot of what's still hard, like long-horizon tasks, reward signals that don't need a human watching, and safety while the robot is learning on the job, sits right at the junction of those two.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the two releases did two different jobs, and it's worth separating them.

Pi 0.5 was really about one word: generalization. Before it, the honest criticism of VLA models was that they were impressive demos that only worked in the lab where the data was collected. Physical Intelligence took a robot into homes it had never seen, kitchens and bedrooms that weren't in the training set, and had it clean up, make a bed, put dishes away. It wasn't flawless, but it was the first time I felt the field had a credible answer to "does this transfer?" The key insight was that the gap isn't closed by more robot data alone. They used co-training across many sources at once: mobile manipulator data, static-arm data, web-scale vision-language data, and high-level subtask prediction, so the model learns semantic understanding of a scene from cheaper sources and only needs robot data to learn how to act. That reframed the data problem for everyone.

Pi 0.6 and the starred variant clarified something else, which is reliability and the move from "can it do the task once" to "can it do the task all day." The headline was recap, the reinforcement-learning-from-experience loop: deploy the policy, collect its own successes and failures with sparse human corrections and rewards, train on that, redeploy. Running espresso machines for hours, folding laundry continuously, assembling boxes. Throughput roughly doubled and failure rates dropped by half or more on those tasks. That matters because a 70 percent success rate is a demo and a 97 percent rate is a product. It showed that the imitation-learning ceiling isn't the real ceiling. You can keep climbing by learning on-policy from the robot's own experience, which is exactly the recipe that made language models work.

So if I had to summarize what 2025 clarified: the recipe is now visible. Pretrain broadly on heterogeneous data for generalization, then specialize through RL on real deployment experience for reliability. The open questions shifted too. It's no longer "will foundation models work for robots." It's how fast the data flywheel spins, how much of this is dexterity versus common sense, and whether the economics of deploying fleets to collect experience close before the funding does. That's a much more engineering-shaped frontier than we had a year earlier, and I think that's healthy.

astra-6.text:
I’d frame it as a shift from asking, “Can a robot perform this task?” to asking, “What lets it perform reliably when the situation changes?” But I should qualify that: we haven’t established what distinguishes Pi 0.5 from the Pi 0.6 variants, so I wouldn’t attach specific capabilities or results to those names here.

The distinction I’d want to explore is between an impressive demonstration and a dependable system. Can it handle an unfamiliar object or environment? Can it recover when an action doesn’t work? How much human intervention does it need to finish the job?

That’s how I’d assess whether those systems clarified the frontier in 2025: whether they helped us identify which of those barriers had moved, and which still stood between a successful demo and useful everyday operation.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d frame the question around the gap between an impressive demonstration and a robot you can actually depend on. But I’d want to be precise about what you mean by Pi 0.6-* before attributing particular results to it.

For me, the key questions would be: Can the robot handle a setting it hasn’t seen before? Can it recover when an action goes wrong? And can it complete a long task without someone stepping in? Those are different from asking whether it can perform a familiar skill once.

So, to say how those releases clarified the frontier in 2025, I’d want to compare them along those dimensions. Did they expand what robots could do, or make those capabilities more reliable? That distinction is central to understanding the progress.
